title: Working into the back bump of a chain
subtitle: How to insert the hook into the back ridge of the foundation chain for a neater first row
excerpt: The back bump of a chain is the ridge on the underside of each chain link. Working into it rather than the top loops gives the foundation row a finished edge that matches the last row.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: The single loop that runs along the underside (back ridge) of the foundation chain, distinct from the two loops on the top face of the chain.
The initial row of chain stitches that forms the starting edge of a flat piece, providing the base into which the first row of stitches is worked.

aliases: working into back of chain crochet

content.text: produces a first row where both edges look the same: a row of V-shapes at the bottom to match the V-shapes at the top. The standard method of working into the top loops of the chain leaves the bottom edge with a visible chain ridge that looks different from the last row. The back bump method is used for flat scarves, blanket strips, and any piece where both long edges will be visible.

Turn the foundation chain over so the underside faces up. The back bump is the single loop that runs along the centre of the chain like a backbone. Each chain link has one bump. The bumps are sometimes easier to see by holding the chain up to a light, or by running a fingernail along the underside.
Working the first row into back bumps
Work the foundation chain and turning chain as normal.
Turn the chain so the underside faces you.
Insert the hook into the back bump of the first chain, not into the top V.
Work the stitch as stated in the pattern. Continue into the back bump of each remaining chain.
From the second row onward, work into the top loops of each stitch as normal. Only the first row uses the back bump.

Use the back bump method when both long edges of the piece will be seen (scarves, washcloths, strips for joining) or when the pattern explicitly instructs it. For most garment pieces where the foundation edge will be seamed or finished with an edging, the standard method is fine.

items.symptom: The back bumps are impossible to find in the chain
items.cause: The chain is worked too tightly and the bumps are compressed against the top loops.
items.fix: Work the foundation chain one hook size larger than the project hook. Looser chains are easier to work into.

items.symptom: The first row is much tighter than subsequent rows
items.cause: Inserting through the single back bump rather than two top loops gives the hook less room.
items.fix: Use a larger hook for the foundation chain, or ease the tension slightly when drawing up the loop in each stitch.

content.text: Work a 20-stitch swatch twice: once working into the top loops of the foundation chain, and once into the back bumps. Hold them side by side to compare the two bottom edges. The difference shows when the extra step is worth taking.
